messages.subject: B-Splines
parts:
Hello all,

I've started work on implementing B-splines in Stan. With Bob's help I've been able to write a function bspline function that is "working" (i.e. agrees with other results but isn't completely tested). This lets me write things in the model/transformed parameters blocks like

ymean[i] <- bspline(P, x[i], beta, knots);

to assign ymean[i] the value of an order P B-spline curve evaluated at x with coefficients beta and knot vector knots. I've attached my first pass at this function.

Since I'm not terribly familiar with Stan's internals I have some implementation questions:

1) How do I check that the knots are ordered and distinct? Is there an appropriate stan::math::validate function or something?

2) If x and the knots are given as data, the correct thing to do is not to use the function above but to precompute a design matrix a la bs() in R. Of course users could do this in R, but it would be nice to have something like

W <- bspline_design(P, X, knots);

in the transformed parameters block and this is straightforward to implement. However, that W matrix is very sparse - at any x there are at most P nonzero basis functions in the B-spline expansion. So If the knot vector is long then it might be worthwhile to just store the P nonzero basis functions and an integer index into the knot/beta vectors. On a long shot, is there an existing data structure for something like that? Or are Eigen's sparse vectors coming?

3) My original need for this functionality came from a project where I have missing x's and varying knots. I got this working in the transformed parameters block using the same method as in the attached header file (this is the standard method for computing B splines).

But I suspect I'm hosing part of the gradient when I find x's location in the knot vector - is that true? There are other ways to compute B splines that might not have the same problem, although they are less efficient. In any event, I can compute the gradient myself; in x it's an order P-1 B-spline, and the in the knots it's another B spline as well, and I'm hoping to implement that at some point too. Of course, 2) is much more straightforward, and probably the most useful to the largest number of people.

src/test/math/error_handling/matrix/check_ordered_test.cpp:#include <stan/math/error_handling/matrix/check_ordered.hpp>

2) If x and the knots are given as data, the correct thing to do is not to use the function above but to precompute a design matrix a la bs() in R. Of course users could do this in R, but it would be nice to have something like

W <- bspline_design(P, X, knots);

in the transformed parameters block and this is straightforward to implement. However, that W matrix is very sparse - at any x there are at most P nonzero basis functions in the B-spline expansion. So If the knot vector is long then it might be worthwhile to just store the P nonzero basis functions and an integer index into the knot/beta vectors. On a long shot, is there an existing data structure for something like that? Or are Eigen's sparse vectors coming?

There are no sparse operations now and it could easily be years before anything like that is implemented. I think if Stan multiplies something by a zero constant, it at least knows not to add to the auto-diff tree. You could write a function that inputs such a W and returns a ymean vector where you could internally do some tricks to speed up the computation. That is probably third or fourth order though.

3) My original need for this functionality came from a project where I have missing x's and varying knots. I got this working in the transformed parameters block using the same method as in the attached header file (this is the standard method for computing B splines).

But I suspect I'm hosing part of the gradient when I find x's location in the knot vector - is that true? There are other ways to compute B splines that might not have the same problem, although they are less efficient. In any event, I can compute the gradient myself; in x it's an order P-1 B-spline, and the in the knots it's another B spline as well, and I'm hoping to implement that at some point too. Of course, 2) is much more straightforward, and probably the most useful to the largest number of people.

As far as I can tell, you are not misleading the auto-differ, although you can try your model in test gradient mode to compare with numeric derivatives. Do you have a reference for this way of handling missing covariates? In any event, being able to do parts of the gradient analytically can lead to a nice boost in performance.

Ben

messages.author: 1b8e6e37275d5083
messages.subject: Re: B-Splines
parts:
Thanks Ben. My concern about the autodiff was the line search; obviously everything else is pretty simple. I should have mentioned that I did test the gradient in x against R code I had handy, and it was fine (up to rounding errors). I haven't got known-good code for the knot gradient just yet so test gradient mode should be handy.

No reference for missing covariates, it's part of a new model in my dissertation. In principle there's nothing special about the missing x's - they get a prior and are sampled like everything else. Analytic gradients for everything are my ultimate goal but will have to wait at least a week or two for me to defend said dissertation :)

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: B-Splines
parts:
A good way to test the auto-diff is with finite
differences on the double-based version of the
function. There are various examples in the code now
that do finite difference tests. I'm about to abstract
the finite difference operation using functionals
on functors, so not every test needs to reimplement
finite diffs.

For (2), there are various ways to implement sparse
and/or ragged structures. For example, a sparse
matrix A can be set up parallel arrays

int r[N];
int c[N];
real v[N];

so that

v[n] == A[r[n], c[n]]

There are, unfortunately, no built-in ways to manipulate
such structures using matrix ops. Ben's right about
it not being at the top of our priority list.

Great projects for someone to take on would be sparse
matrices and ragged arrays.

The dropping rules for terms are pretty sparse, and at the
moment, we don't drop terms that are multiplied by zero. Maybe
we should be doing that --- it depends how common it is going to be.
We do drop 0 under addition and 1 under multiplication.

- Bob
